parts.title: Booking adult swimming lessons
parts.context: A man phones a leisure centre about swimming lessons.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a man phoning a leisure centre to ask about adult swimming lessons. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: Parkside Leisure Centre, Hannah speaking.

script.speaker: vikram
script.text: Hello. I'd like some information about swimming lessons, please. They're for me. I'm afraid I never learned as a child.

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: No problem at all. Lots of adults learn. I'll take some details first.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The lessons are for the caller himself, so 'himself' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: Could I have your name, please?

script.speaker: vikram
script.text: Vikram Nair. That's N-A-I-R.

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: Thank you, Mr Nair. And how old are you, if you don't mind my asking?

script.speaker: vikram
script.text: Forty-two. I know it's late to start, but better late than never.

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: Not at all. Can you swim at all, or are you a complete beginner?

script.speaker: vikram
script.text: A complete beginner. I can stand in the shallow end, but that's about all.

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: And what made you decide to learn now?

script.speaker: vikram
script.text: I'm going to Greece next summer with some friends, and they all swim and sail. I don't want to be left on the beach.

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: Which evenings suit you?

script.speaker: vikram
script.text: Thursdays, if possible. On Mondays I work late, and on Wednesdays I have a class.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: We have three courses. The Beginners' course lasts eight weeks, and it's on Thursday evenings, which suits you. It costs sixty pounds in total.

script.speaker: vikram
script.text: That sounds right. What comes after that?

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: The Improvers' course is for people who can already swim a width. It's six weeks, on Wednesday evenings, and it costs fifty pounds.

script.speaker: vikram
script.text: And if I find the group too slow?

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: You could try the one-to-one lessons. You buy a block of five, and each lesson costs twenty-five pounds. The times are arranged with the teacher.

script.speaker: vikram
script.text: I'll start with the group course. Can I book now?

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: Yes. I'll put you down for the next course, which starts on the third of April. Please bring a towel and goggles, and a swimming hat is compulsory.

script.speaker: vikram
script.text: Thank you. I'll bring a card to pay the deposit.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A new community swimming pool
parts.context: A manager tells members about a new pool.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear a manager telling members about a new community swimming pool. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: osei
script.text: Good evening, everyone, and welcome to the opening of the new Millfield Pool. I'm Grace Osei, the manager, and I'd like to tell you what you can expect.

script.speaker: osei
script.text: The building work took eighteen months. We had hoped to finish in a year, but the wet winter caused delays, and I'm grateful to the neighbours for being so patient.

script.speaker: osei
script.text: The main pool is twenty-five metres long, with six lanes. Next to it is the teaching pool, which has a moving floor. It can be raised for young children and lowered for adults, so one pool serves all ages.

script.speaker: osei
script.text: A single adult swim costs three pounds fifty, and children pay half. Members get a reduced price, and I'll explain the membership in a moment.

script.speaker: osei
script.text: We open every day except Monday, which is kept for cleaning and maintenance. On the other days, the pool is open from seven in the morning until ten at night.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: osei
script.text: We have a lot of activities for older people. There's aqua aerobics on Tuesday and Friday mornings, which is gentle exercise in the water, and a lane swimming session for the over-sixties every weekday at nine. We also teach diving, but that is for young people only, and there's no water polo yet.

script.speaker: osei
script.text: A few rules. Everyone must take a shower before entering the pool. It's not just a matter of cleanliness. It also reduces the chemicals we need to add to the water.

script.speaker: osei
script.text: Parents are welcome to stay during children's lessons, and they can watch from the viewing gallery above the teaching pool, where there's a café as well. The gym is for members only.

script.speaker: osei
script.text: To join, the easiest way is online, through our website, where you can pay by card and collect your membership card at the desk. You can also join at reception, but the queue is often long on Saturdays. Now, shall we cut the ribbon?

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A pendulum experiment
parts.context: Two physics students plan their lab report.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two physics students, Greta and Sanjay, discussing their report on a pendulum experiment. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: greta
script.text: Sanjay, have you looked at the results from our pendulum experiment? I've put them in a table.

script.speaker: sanjay
script.text: Yes. The aim was to find out how the length of the string affects the time of one swing. I think the report should say that clearly in the introduction.

script.speaker: greta
script.text: Agreed. One thing bothers me. The results for the longest string look odd. The time was shorter than we expected.

script.speaker: sanjay
script.text: I think the string stretched as the mass hung from it. We used cotton, which isn't ideal. A thin wire would have been better.

script.speaker: greta
script.text: Should we repeat the experiment?

script.speaker: sanjay
script.text: There isn't time. The lab is only booked until Wednesday, and Dr Frost wants the report by Friday.

script.speaker: greta
script.text: We did measure each length three times and take the average, so at least that reduces random errors.

script.speaker: sanjay
script.text: Yes, and what will the graph show?

script.speaker: greta
script.text: The length on one axis, and the square of the time on the other. It should be a straight line, if the theory is right.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: greta
script.text: Now the method. Let me describe it step by step. First, we attached a piece of string to a stand, with a small mass at the end.

script.speaker: sanjay
script.text: Then we measured the length with a ruler, from the pivot to the middle of the mass.

script.speaker: greta
script.text: Next we pulled the mass back to an angle of ten degrees, which we measured with a protractor, so that every swing began in the same way.

script.speaker: sanjay
script.text: We released it and timed ten complete swings with a stopwatch, because one swing is too quick to time accurately.

script.speaker: greta
script.text: And finally we plotted the results on a graph, and drew a line of best fit.

script.speaker: sanjay
script.text: That's a clear description. I'll add the diagram.

script.speaker: greta
script.text: Thanks. I'll start on the conclusion.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: how rainbows form
parts.context: A physics lecture on the formation of rainbows.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about how rainbows form. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good morning. Few things in nature are as admired as the rainbow, and yet most people cannot say exactly how one forms. So let's look at it step by step.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: A rainbow needs two things: sunlight and raindrops. When a ray of sunlight enters a raindrop, it slows down and bends. This bending is called refraction. The ray then travels across the drop and is reflected from the back of it, like a mirror.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: When the ray leaves the drop, it bends again. And here is the key point. Sunlight is white, but it is really a mixture of colours, and each colour bends by a slightly different amount. So the white light is split into its different colours, and we see them spread across the sky.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Red light leaves the drop at an angle of about forty-two degrees to the direction of the sun's rays, and violet at a slightly smaller angle. That is why red is always on the outside of the bow and violet on the inside.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: To see a rainbow, you need the sun behind you, with the rain in front of you. The sun must also be low in the sky, so rainbows are most common in the early morning and late afternoon. If the sun is higher than forty-two degrees, the rainbow falls below the horizon, and you cannot see it from the ground.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: In fact, a rainbow is really a full circle. From the ground we see only the top half, but from an aircraft, you can sometimes see the whole circle, with the shadow of the plane in the middle.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Sometimes there is a second, fainter rainbow outside the first. Its colours are in the reverse order, with red on the inside, because the light has been reflected twice. The sky between the two bows looks darker than the rest, which is a real effect and not an illusion.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: And you don't need rain. Rainbows can be seen in the spray of a waterfall, or a garden hose, as long as the sun is in the right place. Next week we'll look at halos around the sun.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
